variants.name: async/await compiler state machine (TAP)
variants.implementation_notes: C# absorbs the ACT into the language: an async method compiles to a state machine (IAsyncStateMachine.MoveNext) whose continuation and captured locals are the completion token, and awaiting a Task demultiplexes exactly that continuation when the producer completes it - no token table, no lookup by request identity. Write the classic structure by hand only where an operation completes outside any async method (see the TaskCompletionSource and APM variants); for pooled hot paths IValueTaskSource<TResult> is the allocation-free, version-stamped form, but the documented default is Task unless profiling justifies it.
pitfalls: Continuations may run on the thread that completes the token: without TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously a completion handler can block or re-enter the completing I/O thread.
Racing completers must use TrySetResult/TrySetException; a second Set* fails, so a losing path that used Set* discovers the race as an exception.
ValueTask<TResult> may be awaited only once and pooled IValueTaskSource<TResult> implementations carry a version stamp - re-awaiting a recycled pooled token reads another operation's result.
APM interop: calling the End* method twice with the same IAsyncResult is undefined, and AsyncState is an untyped object that must be downcast and must not outlive the operation.

variants.name: TaskCompletionSource<TResult> (producer-side token)
variants.implementation_notes: For operations that complete on their own schedule - event handlers, native callbacks, a protocol reply arriving on a socket loop - TaskCompletionSource is the explicit ACT: the consumer keeps the .Task half while the completing side holds the source and calls TrySetResult/TrySetException once. This is where the pattern's registry discipline still applies in C#: when the completing side cannot close over the source, keep a registry keyed by the request and remove the entry on completion, timeout and cancellation.
pitfalls: A TaskCompletionSource is not a completion queue: a second TrySet* is silently ignored, so a registration that fires repeatedly needs its own multiplicity handling.
Sources kept in a registry without removal retain their continuation graph - remove on completion, timeout and cancellation.

variants.name: IAsyncResult.AsyncState (APM interop)
variants.idiom_name: Begin*/End* pair with the AsyncState token
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's literal .NET ancestor, still met when wrapping a legacy API (Task.Factory.FromAsync): BeginOperationName takes a state object that the runtime passes back to the AsyncCallback as IAsyncResult.AsyncState, and EndOperationName collects the result. It is a pointer-style ACT with no type safety - keep the state object small, cast once, and pair every Begin with exactly one End.
pitfalls: If the callback throws before End* runs, the operation's resources stay unreleased; always complete the Begin/End pair on every path.
The state object lives until the callback runs - a state object holding large buffers turns abandoned operations into memory growth.
